subject: Beginner question - layout of point transect data in Distance?

messages.subject: Beginner question - layout of point transect data in Distance?
parts:
Hello,

I'm going to use Distance to analyze point transect data, which I have never done before (have only done line transects in the past). I want to make sure I'm on the right track when it comes to entering data into Distance for this purpose. I have included a screenshot of some sample data below, for reference.


In my example, I have named my transects gs-001, gs-002, and gs-003. Each of these transects consists of points, spaced 100 m apart, from which biologists conduct surveys. My first question is, should I be listing the actual transects here, as I have, or should I be listing the individual points?

Second question: We visited each transect three times, so is it okay to have the survey effort be '3'? I'm thinking that if I leave it as '1,' I would then have to use a multiplier somewhere down the line?

Radial distance seems straightforward, but my final question is this: What if someone detected the same individual of a target species from more than one point along the transect? For example, they saw a hawk perched on a post when they were at the first point along the transect, and the hawk was still there when the observer arrived at the second point along the transect. That would only get recorded once per line transect, of course, and could be recorded more than once if seen from multiple line transects, but I'm wondering how this is dealt with for point transects?

Thanks in advance, I always appreciate everyone's expertise in this forum.

Best,
Nick Peterson

messages.subject: {Disarmed} Re: [distance-sampling] Beginner question - layout of point transect data in Distance?
parts:
Nick

Nice to hear from you again.  Short answers to some of your questions:
  • your data set-up is correct.  The sampling unit is the point; the transects are merely a way of getting from one to the next; no sampling is taking place while in transit.  Hence it need not be reflected in your data organisation..
  • Representing effort as the number of visits is just right and does avoid the need for a multiplier.  Another advantage of using the effort field rather than a multiplier is that gives flexibility should not all points be visited an equal number of times (if there were fewer crew available for a visit or if a pesky bear prevents visits to some points on a scheduled visit).
  • Detections of an individual from multiple points might be thought to cause problems.  The situation you describe, where you know it is the same individual, probably best to only record the first detection.  The situation is probably more subtle--detections are made by sound, how to know if it is the same individual? I draw your attention to the 2006 Auk paper by Prof. Buckland in which he conducted a simulation study to examine exactly this situation:
    • Buckland, Stephen T. 2006. Point-transect surveys for songbirds: robust methodologies. The Auk 123 (2): 345–57. MailScanner has detected a possible fraud attempt from "link.getmailspring.com" claiming to be https://doi.org/10.1642/0004-8038(2006)123[345:PSFSRM]2.0.CO;2.

      The punchline paragraph of that paper relevant to your question is:
      "For population 2, there was severe overlap between plots, so that most birds in the study area were detected more than once. On average, there were 356 detections from a population of 225 birds, of which only 100 birds were within the central 1-km square that was surveyed. Nevertheless, there was almost no bias in estimated bird density: true density was one bird ha–1, and the mean of the 1,000 estimated densities was 1.0056 ± 0.0026 birds ha–1 (mean ± SE). There was also only mild underestimation of the standard error: true standard error (estimated by the standard deviation of the 1,000 population size estimates) was 0.0815, whereas the mean of the 1,000 analytic standard errors was 0.0750.
Have a serious read of the Auk paper section dealing with overlapping points.
